description: Expanded RAG evaluation dataset (25 questions) based on PA-EIS (Priority-Aware Edge Inference Scheduling) IEEE paper. Includes original 10 questions from baseline benchmark plus 15 new questions for within-paper validation.

questions.question: What is the main motivation for studying containerised Linux edge nodes?
questions.notes: Tests understanding of paper's core research motivation

questions.question: What methodology does PA-EIS use?
questions.notes: Tests extraction of technical approach

questions.question: What workloads are used for evaluation?
questions.notes: Tests identification of experimental workloads

questions.question: What are the reported evaluation results or metrics?
questions.notes: Tests handling of explicitly missing information

questions.question: What limitations does the paper explicitly mention?
questions.notes: Tests extraction of stated limitations

questions.question: What Linux kernel features does PA-EIS rely on?
questions.notes: Tests identification of specific technical dependencies

questions.question: Why does the evaluation intentionally restrict CPU cores?
questions.notes: Tests understanding of experimental design rationale

questions.question: What container technology is used and what does it enable?
questions.notes: Tests ability to connect related information

questions.question: How does PA-EIS differ from traditional OS scheduling approaches?
questions.notes: Tests synthesis across multiple chunks

questions.question: What is the paper's stance on neural architecture search?
questions.notes: Tests proper handling of out-of-scope questions

questions.question: What is the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) and what problem does it create?
questions.notes: Tests understanding of background technical concepts. CFS is described on pages 1-2 as the Linux CPU scheduler that allocates time proportionally to weight but has no semantic understanding of task priorities.

questions.question: What are the three research questions (RQs) that PA-EIS addresses?
questions.notes: Tests extraction of structured research questions. The paper explicitly states RQ1 (background task degradation), RQ2 (tail latency with contention), and RQ3 (user-space policy effectiveness).

questions.question: What is the layered architecture of the experimental edge node?
questions.notes: Tests extraction of system architecture. Figure 1 on page 2 describes the four-layer architecture: L1 (physical resources), L2 (Linux kernel), L3 (container runtime), L4 (workloads), plus instrumentation plane.

questions.question: What is virtual runtime and how does CFS use it?
questions.notes: Tests deep understanding of CFS mechanism. Page 2 describes how heavier tasks accrue virtual time more slowly, causing them to be selected more often and preempted less readily.

questions.question: What hardware platform is used for the experiments?
questions.notes: Tests identification of hardware platform. The paper repeatedly mentions 'single commodity Linux host' and 'CPU-only' evaluation with no accelerator hardware.

questions.question: Why doesn't the paper use accelerator hardware in its evaluation?
questions.notes: Tests understanding of experimental design choices. The paper explains that accelerators bypass CPU scheduling contention, which is the object of study, thus requiring CPU-only evaluation.

questions.question: What metrics are used to evaluate inference latency?
questions.notes: Tests extraction of evaluation metrics. The paper focuses on both mean and tail latency, specifically mentioning 99th percentiles.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the parameter sweep in the evaluation?
questions.notes: Tests understanding of experimental methodology. The paper describes sweeping scheduling weight and nice value over a grid to understand the shape of the latency relationship, not just two-point comparison.

questions.question: What does PA-EIS stand for and what does it do?
questions.notes: Tests basic system identification. PA-EIS (Priority-Aware Edge Inference Scheduling) is explicitly defined and described as a user-space policy that uses cgroup weights to control tail latency.

questions.question: What background tasks are used alongside inference workloads?
questions.notes: Tests identification of experimental workload composition. The paper mentions CPU loop and I/O logger as background tasks running alongside inference workloads to create contention.

questions.question: What is TFLite and why is it used?
questions.notes: Tests identification of technical tools. TFLite (TensorFlow Lite) is mentioned as the inference framework used for running the models.

questions.question: What problem arises when edge inference runs on general-purpose operating systems?
questions.notes: Tests synthesis of problem statement. The paper explains that CFS treats all tasks fairly without understanding latency sensitivity, causing background tasks to interfere with inference.

questions.question: What instrumentation tools are mentioned for measuring system behavior?
questions.notes: Tests extraction of specific technical tools. Page 2 Figure 1 caption lists instrumentation tools: perf, /proc and /sys, cpu.stat, RAPL, timestamps.

questions.question: How many repetitions are performed per parameter point in the experiment?
questions.notes: Tests extraction of specific numerical detail. Page 1 explicitly states 'thirty repetitions per point' in the parameter sweep.

questions.question: What is the relationship between edge AI and data center inference mentioned in the paper?
questions.notes: Tests understanding of broader context. Page 1 motivation explains that inference has moved from data center to edge for practical reasons: round trips to remote endpoints are unacceptable for interactive workloads.
